# Fast and slow: System One models and Jev {#sec-ch06}

When TypeSafe AI released Jev, it did not call it a better LLM. It called it the first of a new type of model, a *System One* model [@typesafe2026]. In this chapter we first see what this name means and why it is useful. Then we look at what is really known about Jev, and what is only claimed.

::: {.goals}
- The idea of fast and slow thinking, in people and in software.
- How to let a fast model handle easy cases and send only doubtful ones to a slow model.
- How to judge a company's claims about a new AI model.
:::

## Two ways of thinking

What is 2 + 2? The answer came to you immediately. Now try 17 × 24. This feels different: you have to stop and work it out step by step.

People often call these two ways of thinking **System 1** (fast and automatic) and **System 2** (slow and careful). Most of daily life runs on System 1, and it is usually right. We use System 2 only for the few things that need real effort.

Software has the same two kinds:

- **Fast tools**, like simple rules and small models, answer in a fraction of a second and cost almost nothing. They are good at familiar, repeated cases.
- **Slow tools**, like LLMs that "think" step by step before answering, can handle almost anything, but they take seconds and you pay for every word they write.

In real work, most decisions are quick and repeated many times a day: "Is this alert real?", "Which team gets this ticket?" Only a few need deep thinking, like writing an incident report (@fig-task-map). Yet today, many companies send everything to slow LLMs.

![Tasks in a security team, placed by how often they happen and how much thinking they need (illustrative). Most frequent tasks are quick judgements, shown at the bottom right. The few tasks that need real thinking happen rarely.](/figures/ch15/task-map.pdf){#fig-task-map}

::: {.keyidea}
**Most daily decisions are quick ones, but we use slow, expensive AI for all of them.** Like a cashier who does not need a calculator for 2 + 2, most decisions need a fast answer. Keep the slow, careful AI for the few hard cases.
:::

## Send only the doubtful cases to the slow system

Think of a busy hospital. A nurse at the front desk sees every patient quickly. Most cases are clear: a small cut, a routine check-up. The nurse sends only the unclear cases to the senior doctor. The doctor's time is used where it matters, and nobody waits for hours.

AI systems can work the same way: a fast model sees every case, and only the cases it is unsure about go to the slow, expensive model.

How much does this help? Suppose sending *every* alert to the slow model would give the best possible result. At Kestrel:

- Sending only the 20% of alerts the fast model was least sure about gave {{< num ch15 share_gain_20 pct >}} of that best result.
- Sending a random 20% of alerts gave only {{< num ch15 share_gain_20_random pct >}} (@fig-routing-curve).

So choosing *which* cases to send matters far more than how many you send. And you pay the slow cost for only 20% of the alerts.

![Total cost per day as more alerts go to the slow model. Sending the alerts the fast model is least sure about (green, solid line) gives most of the benefit early. Sending a random share (grey, dashed line) helps very little until almost everything is sent.](/figures/ch15/routing-curve.pdf){#fig-routing-curve}

::: {.keyidea}
**Let a fast model handle the easy cases, and send only the doubtful ones to the slow one.** If the fast model really knows when it is unsure, you get almost the full quality while paying the slow cost for only a few cases.
:::

This works only if the fast checker knows when it is unsure. A good nurse says, "I'm not sure about this one; let the doctor see it." A bad one is confidently wrong. For a model, this means its numbers must be correct: when it says "50%", the case really must be a toss-up (Chapter 2).

Fast judgement, by a person or a model, works best when the same kinds of cases keep coming, there is plenty of practice, and you soon find out whether you were right. Sorting security alerts fits this well. Predicting share prices does not.

## What we know about Jev: three groups

When this book was written, Jev was new, and only some companies could use it. So how can we judge it? Think of buying a used car. Some things you check yourself on a test drive. Some things only the seller tells you, like how far it has been driven. And some things nobody can tell you yet, like how it will run next winter. It is wise to keep these three groups separate. We can do the same for Jev.

**What you can check yourself: how it is used.** You send Jev a short description of the situation and a few clear questions. For each question, you get back an answer with a probability for every option. There are three types of question: yes/no, pick one, and rate on a scale (Chapter 7).

**What the company says, but nobody outside has proved:**

- Jev answers all your questions together in one quick step, instead of writing word by word like an LLM. TypeSafe says this is why it is fast.
- Jev is trained to give correct probabilities, using a method TypeSafe calls **RLCD**. The details are not public. The idea is reasonable, because a model can be trained so that correct numbers get the best score.

**What nobody outside the company knows yet:**

- how big the model is and what data it learned from;
- whether its numbers are correct on *your* data;
- how it behaves when an attacker writes the text it reads;
- how much it changes from one version to the next.

These unknowns are exactly the things you most need to know before you trust a model with real decisions.

::: {.keyidea}
**For any new AI product, separate what is proven from what is only claimed.** Put each claim in one of three groups: checked by you, said by the company, or unknown. This protects you from advertising hype.
:::

## Check if the company's numbers agree

Here is what TypeSafe reports, and what it means in practice:

- **Speed:** about 70 to 500 milliseconds per answer, which is less than half a second.
- **Price:** \$0.042 for every million tokens it reads, and nothing extra for its answers.
- **Cost of a million decisions**, if each needs about 500 tokens of description: about **\$21** with Jev, against about **\$660** with an example mid-range LLM.

LLM prices vary a lot, so treat this only as a rough guide. And for any claim that something is "faster", always ask: *faster than what, and for which task?* [@regolo2026]

There is also a simple test anyone can do: when a company gives several numbers, check whether they fit together. In its launch demo, Jev played the video game *Doom*:

1. It made about 10 decisions per second, at a reported cost of \$7 per hour.
2. That is 36,000 decisions per hour, or about \$0.0002 per decision.
3. At the listed price, \$0.0002 pays for about 4,600 tokens of game description per decision, which is a sensible amount.

The numbers fit together. This does not prove they are true, but if they had not fitted, we would have learned something important.

The unknowns about a new model are not a reason to avoid it. They are a reason to test it on your own data before you trust it.

::: {.breaks}
System 1 and System 2 are only a simple way to describe thinking; they are not two real parts of the brain. A System One model also has no real "intuition"; it is a learned formula. Sending doubtful cases to the slow system works only if the fast system knows when it is unsure. When a completely new kind of case appears, the fast system may be confidently wrong, and only random checks will catch it. Finally, the company's numbers come from its own tests, and a new model can change quickly, so fix a version and test it yourself.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. List five decisions in your own work that are quick System 1 judgements, and two that need slow System 2 thinking. What makes them different?
:::
